about: Call It fixtures: generated instances in the shape packages/generators produces (InstanceBase and KeyBase), for GEN-call-it's four templates. Each fact is a verdict line of the run its stem cites. The component's tests render them, and GATE-items reads them through its own instance reader (scripts/spikes/W1-T07/lib/items-gate.mjs).

item.stem: An agent's guarded transfer checks `amount <= b`, the recipient's balance, where it should check the sender's. Over `Int`, Z3 is asked for a transfer that passes the guard and leaves the sender below zero {{run:RUN-z3-boot-variant}}.

options.why: A small linear integer query is decided outright.

origin.operator: read a decided query as undecided

options.why: The guard bounds the amount by the recipient's balance, so a transfer of 1 from an account holding 0 passes it and overdraws the sender.
This reads the guard as protecting the sender; it protects nothing about the sender's balance.

item.stem: The transfer has no guard. Z3 is asked whether both balances can end below zero at once: `a2 < 0 and b2 < 0` {{run:RUN-z3-demorgan}}.

options.why: The transfer is unguarded, but the recipient only gains, so both balances cannot fall.

origin.operator: a wrong negation carried into the encoding

options.why: Three linear integer constraints are decided outright.

origin.operator: read a decided query as undecided

options.why: No input gives the recipient a negative balance, so Z3 answers `unsat`; the property is still violated, and the right negation uses `or`.

item.stem: Z3 is asked whether two whole numbers `x` and `y` exist with `x**y == 8` and `y > 1` {{run:RUN-z3-unknown-pow}}.

options.why: Z3 gives up on a nonlinear exponent, and the reason line says why.
A solution exists, but a verdict reports this run, not the truth.

origin.operator: a verdict read as the truth

options.why: A solution exists, so a guess of `unsat` misread the constraint.

origin.operator: a wrong operator carried into the encoding

item.stem: TLC will check the DoubleSpend model (Init = 100, Amount = 80, two workers) with `-deadlock`, for the invariant `NoOverspend` {{run:RUN-tlc-doublespend}}.

parts.prompt: If TLC finds a violation, how many actions long is the counterexample it prints?

options.why: Each worker reads the balance and then writes it, and the second write is the one that overspends, so fewer than four actions cannot reach the violation.
The counterexample has 5 states, which is 4 actions: the first worker reads, the second reads, the first writes, the second writes {{run:RUN-tlc-doublespend}}.
A shortest counterexample cannot be longer than the search is deep, and TLC reports a depth of 5 {{run:RUN-tlc-doublespend}}.

item.stem: On PostgreSQL 18.6 at REPEATABLE READ, an invariant says the team total never goes below zero. Two transactions each read the total (200), each withdraws 150 from a different account, and both commit {{run:RUN-pg-anomalies}}.

parts.prompt: The team total ends at -100. Which anomaly is this?

options.why: A lost update overwrites a value another transaction wrote; here each transaction withdraws from a different account, so no write is overwritten.

origin.operator: which anomaly the isolation level allows

options.why: A dirty read sees data that was never committed; both transactions read the committed total.

origin.operator: which anomaly the isolation level allows

options.why: Each check held on its own snapshot, and together the two withdrawals broke the invariant: the team total reaches -100 {{run:RUN-pg-anomalies}}.
A non-repeatable read means one transaction reads the same row twice and sees different values; neither transaction reads twice.

origin.operator: which anomaly the isolation level allows

item.stem: On PostgreSQL 18.6 at READ COMMITTED, two transactions each read the balance (100), then each runs an update that writes the balance it read minus 80 {{run:RUN-pg-anomalies}}.

parts.prompt: The final balance is 20, although 160 was spent from 100. Which anomaly is this?

options.why: Write skew needs two transactions that write different rows after reading the same data; here both write the same row.

origin.operator: which anomaly the isolation level allows

options.why: Both writes used the value each had read, so the second overwrote the first: final balance 20, 160 spent from 100 {{run:RUN-pg-anomalies}}.
A dirty read sees data that was never committed; both transactions read the committed balance.

origin.operator: which anomaly the isolation level allows

options.why: A phantom read is a set of rows changing between two reads of the same predicate; no predicate is re-read here.

origin.operator: which anomaly the isolation level allows

item.stem: Z3 returned `unknown (canceled)` on a query with no solution, at `rlimit` 5000000 {{run:RUN-z3-budget-pyodide}}.

parts.prompt: Which statements are true of Z3's answers?

statements.text: A `unsat` covers every input of its encoding, if the solver is sound.
statements.why: `unsat` says no model of this query exists, which is a statement about the encoding.
`sat` gives a model of the query, which for a violation query is a witness that the property fails.

origin.operator: sat read as the property holds

statements.why: A stop on the budget is no verdict: the search was cut off before it showed anything either way.

statements.text: A larger `rlimit` could turn this `unknown` into a verdict.
statements.why: The run stopped on its budget, so more budget is the one change that can finish it.

statements.text: A `unsat` over `Int` also covers 64-bit integer code.
statements.why: Over `Int` a negative amount makes the sender richer, while 64-bit arithmetic wraps; the encoding is the claim.

item.stem: Z3 returned `unsat` on the violation query behind a claim whose premises are `a >= 0`, `b >= 0` and `amount > 0`, with the guard `amount <= a` {{run:RUN-z3-vacuous-unsat}}.

parts.prompt: Which statements are true of that result?

statements.text: The result is about this encoding and these premises.
statements.why: A solver answers one query over one encoding; the claim's other parts are separate.

statements.text: The result shows that the premises can all hold at once.
statements.why: `unsat` of the violation query says nothing about the premises being satisfiable; the premise query does.

statements.text: A premise query that returns `sat` shows the claim is about something.
statements.why: A transfer that meets every premise exists, so the claim is not vacuous {{run:RUN-z3-vacuous-unsat}}.

statements.text: With contradictory premises, the violation query would return `sat`.
statements.why: Contradictory premises leave no model, so every violation query is `unsat` and every property is proved vacuously {{run:RUN-z3-vacuous-unsat}}.

origin.operator: a false antecedent read as irrelevant

statements.text: If the solver is sound, no transfer that meets these premises leaves the sender below zero.
statements.why: `unsat` for exactly this encoding means no model of the violation exists, if the solver is sound.
